  "title": "CompSchema-IE: Hard Grammar Constraints vs. Soft Filtering for Zero-Shot Event Argument Extraction — An Empirical Study via Synthetic Supervision",
  "core_problem": "Synthetic-data-based zero-shot event argument extraction (EAE) faces a structural data quality problem that existing approaches address only partially. LtGaE (AAAI 2026) uses soft RL penalties for argument completeness — a quality score penalty that fires when the proportion of empty arguments per sample deviates from a target range [τ−ε, τ+ε], but does not enforce per-role entity-type compatibility or hard cardinality bounds during decoding. Gatto et al. (ACL 2025 Long) uses free-form LLM generation with no formal constraints. FineCSDA (NLPCC 2024) targets the long-tail distribution of argument roles via sample-level augmentation of rare event types (SDAM) and context-level injection of rare role fillers (CDAM), but neither module enforces formal cardinality bounds or entity-type constraints — coverage improvement relies on targeted prompt design rather than any structural enumeration mechanism. GEMS (ACL Findings 2025) applies ontology steering at inference time via multi-perspective prompting and voting, not at training-data generation time.

None of these approaches systematically addresses the structural salience of rare argument roles during generation. The RAMS ontology TSV specifies only maximum cardinality (the 'count permitted' column is an upper bound on role occurrences per instance, not a minimum), so grammar-constrained decoding via XGrammar enforces: (a) no role exceeds its permitted maximum count, and (b) when filled, entity types are compatible. It cannot logically force optional roles to appear — setting min-cardinality=1 for all roles would require an assumption not derivable from the RAMS TSV and would produce unrealistically complete training instances where every event instance has every schema role filled. Instead, Schema-Constrained Grammar (SCG) provides a different mechanism: structural salience. Critically, in the XGrammar encoding all applicable role slots appear as required keys in the output JSON template — the LLM generates an empty string or null value for absent optional arguments but cannot omit role keys from the output. This key-level requirement is the structural salience mechanism: it forces the model's attention to each slot during the forward pass, counteracting the prior bias toward omitting rare slots that characterizes unconstrained generation. Even when individual constraint violation rates are low (plausible for strong instruction-following models like Qwen3-32B), unconstrained generation tends to cluster on high-frequency role patterns due to LLM prior biases, likely under-representing rare optional roles. Post-hoc filtering (Condition B) removes entity-type violations and cardinality overruns but operates on outputs from unconstrained generation where rare role keys were never generated — it cannot recover coverage for roles absent from the unconstrained output corpus.

The primary gap CompSchema-IE targets is empirical and analytical: we do not know (a) whether hard grammar constraints (formal cardinality + entity-type enforcement via XGrammar, which provides structural salience through required role-key enumeration over and above entity-type and cardinality filtering) outperform oracle post-hoc filtering of unconstrained generation on downstream zero-shot EAE, (b) in which role strata these differences concentrate, or (c) whether any structural regularization gains are mechanistically explained by rare-role instantiation improvements. Answering these questions empirically — with a clean three-condition ablation, volume-controlled design, and stratified evaluation — is a concretely useful contribution for EMNLP Findings, even if overall F1 deltas are modest.",
  "opportunity": "The supervised-to-zero-shot gap remains 8–35 F1 points (supervised SOTA: DEGAP COLING 2025 — RAMS 54.2 Arg-C F1, WikiEvents 67.1 Arg-C F1; TSCA IET Software 2026 adds ~+3.0/+1.0 F1 in fully supervised settings; best zero-shot cross-dataset: LtGaE 32–47 F1 on RAMS2RAMS/RAMS2Wiki/Wiki2Wiki). Training data quality for the generator model is a concrete bottleneck: LtGaE's soft RL penalties improve over prior unconstrained generation but cannot guarantee per-role proportional coverage; FineCSDA's targeted augmentation improves rare-role counts but lacks formal structural enumeration. GEMS (ACL Findings 2025) provides ontology-guided inference-time EAE but does not address training-data generation quality. SynthIE (EMNLP 2023) demonstrated that task-reversal generation can produce highly effective synthetic IE training data, but uses no grammar-constrained decoding and does not address event argument extraction. The key open question is whether hard constraints provide a measurable advantage over oracle-quality soft filtering under a volume-controlled design. This question has a clean experimental operationalization: (A) unconstrained generation, (B) unconstrained generation with post-hoc violation filtering (oracle soft constraint approximation, volume-matched to A and C), and (C) grammar-constrained generation via XGrammar — same model, same schema information, same final training volume. If C outperforms B on rare roles despite similar overall violation rates, the result directly demonstrates that structural salience (not just constraint compliance) drives the downstream gain — the SCG's required role-key enumeration in the output template forces the model to instantiate each slot rather than silently omitting rare keys during unconstrained generation. This is a falsifiable, mechanistically interpretable empirical finding — the type EMNLP Findings values.",
  "landscape": "GuideX (ACL Findings 2025) sets SOTA on 7 zero-shot NER benchmarks with Llama-3.1 fine-tuned on generated data, but explicitly does not address event argument extraction.

GEMS (ACL Findings 2025, aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.1353) uses multi-perspective prompts and ontology steering for inference-time EAE on WikiEvents, ACE05, and ERE-EN, achieving SOTA in low-resource settings. GEMS applies ontology knowledge at inference time via a voting mechanism over multiple generation paths with T5-large as the base model; CompSchema-IE instead applies hard grammar constraints at training-data generation time, investigating whether structural salience from required role-key enumeration during generation improves downstream rare-role coverage — a complementary research question targeting a different phase of the pipeline.

FineCSDA ('FineCSDA: Boosting Document-Level Event Argument Extraction with Fine-Grained Data Augmentation', NLPCC 2024, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-981-97-9434-8_1) directly identifies the long-tail distribution of argument roles as a bottleneck and proposes two augmentation modules: SDAM generates new document-level samples for rare event types, and CDAM injects rare argument roles and corresponding context into common event type documents. Unlike CompSchema-IE, FineCSDA does not impose formal cardinality bounds or entity-type constraints, and provides no structural role-slot enumeration — coverage improvement relies on targeted prompt design for rare types and roles.

Gatto et al. ('Document-Level Event-Argument Data Augmentation for Challenging Role Types', ACL 2025 Long, arXiv:2403.03304) is a direct predecessor: LLM-powered augmentation (Mad Lib Aug and Struct2Text) for extractive EAE, +13 F1 on zero-shot role types using BERT-QA, no schema constraints, few-shot cross-domain setting (5 documents per event type available), zero-shot roles within seen event types — not fully zero-shot event type generalization.

BiTer (Information Processing and Management, May 2025, doi:10.1016/j.ipm.2025.104199) achieves +4.6%/+7.5%/+0.4% zero-shot Arg-C F1 on RAMS/WikiEvents/ACE2005 using within-dataset event-type-held-out splits. Protocol is NOT directly comparable to LtGaE's cross-dataset three-way protocol; reported separately with explicit footnote.

LtGaE (AAAI 2026, arXiv:2603.02909) uses multi-agent Propose-Evaluate-Revise with RL reward that includes a soft penalty p_i activated when the proportion of empty arguments ρ_i deviates from a target range [τ−ε, τ+ε] — a global aggregate quality-score adjustment per sample, not a per-role structural enumeration or hard decoding constraint. Achieves 45.77/32.38/46.96 Span-F1 on RAMS2RAMS/RAMS2Wiki/Wiki2Wiki. Does not compare against BiTer.

ASEE (EMNLP Findings 2025, arXiv:2505.08690) addresses inference-time schema selection via RAG; no hard constraints; does not report RAMS/WikiEvents numbers.

BoostCD (EMNLP 2025 Main, arXiv:2506.14901) demonstrates that constrained and unconstrained decoding produce complementary errors at inference time for closed IE (relation extraction), with a learned boosted model combining both for stronger performance. CompSchema-IE investigates an analogous question at training-data generation time for event argument extraction, where structural salience differences compound across a finite corpus rather than being resolved at inference.

SALE (MDPI Electronics, March 2026) uses code-based LLM fine-tuning with RL alignment for cross-task zero-shot transfer; no formal schema constraints during data generation.

Extracting Events Like Code (AAAI 2026, arXiv:2511.13118) uses Python class definitions for inference-time schema validation, not training-data generation.

SynthIE (EMNLP 2023, ACL Anthology 2023.emnlp-main.96) generates synthetic IE training data via task-reversal (structure→text generation), achieving large F1 gains on smaller models; uses no grammar-constrained decoding, no formal cardinality bounds, and targets IE triplets rather than compositional event argument extraction. Establishes the task-reversal generation paradigm that CompSchema-IE extends with hard compositional constraints.

Supervised SOTA: DEGAP (COLING 2025, arXiv:2405.13325) — RAMS 54.2 Arg-C F1, WikiEvents 67.1 Arg-C F1. TSCA (IET Software 2026) adds ~+3.0/+1.0 F1 in fully supervised settings.

The specific open question not addressed by any prior work — including GEMS, FineCSDA, LtGaE, Gatto et al., or BoostCD: does hard grammar constraint enforcement (cardinality + entity-type, XGrammar) — which provides structural salience via required role-key enumeration in the output JSON template — outperform oracle post-hoc filtering of unconstrained generation under a volume-controlled design, and does any advantage concentrate in rare-role and high-cardinality-tightness strata where the structural enumeration mechanism is most likely to shift the LLM's generation distribution?",
  "approach": "CompSchema-IE is framed explicitly as an empirical study targeting EMNLP 2026 Findings. The primary contribution is a clean, volume-controlled three-condition ablation that isolates the value of hard constraint enforcement over soft filtering, combined with a stratified analysis that localizes any gains mechanistically.

**Primary Hypothesis (Structural Salience, Empirically Testable)**:
The RAMS ontology TSV specifies only maximum cardinality (the 'count permitted' column is an upper bound on role occurrences per instance). XGrammar therefore enforces: (a) no role appears more than its permitted maximum count, and (b) when filled, entity types are compatible. It does NOT logically guarantee that optional rare roles appear in every generated instance — this would require setting min-cardinality=1 for all roles, a design choice not derivable from the RAMS TSV alone and one that would produce unrealistically complete training instances where every event instance has every schema role filled.

CompSchema-IE instead adopts the structural salience framing: SCG provides structural salience by explicitly enumerating every applicable role slot as a required key in the constrained generation template. In the XGrammar encoding, all applicable role slots for a given event type appear as required keys in the output JSON template; the LLM generates an empty string or null value for absent optional arguments but cannot omit role keys from the output. This key-level requirement is the mechanism of structural salience: it forces the model's attention to each slot during the forward pass, counteracting the prior bias toward omitting rare slots that characterizes unconstrained generation. Condition B (post-hoc filtering) can remove entity-type violations and cardinality overruns from unconstrained outputs, but cannot recover coverage for role keys that unconstrained generation never emitted in the first place. The structural salience hypothesis is therefore that Condition C will show improved rare-role instantiation over Condition B even when overall constraint violation rates are comparable — an effect logically independent of constraint compliance and attributable specifically to required key enumeration. Even when individual constraint violation rates are low — expected for Qwen3-32B given its strong instruction-following capability — unconstrained generation's prior biases tend to cluster on high-frequency role patterns, under-representing rare optional roles. FineCSDA (NLPCC 2024) partially addresses rare-role under-representation via targeted prompting (SDAM/CDAM), but without formal structural enumeration; CompSchema-IE's SCG provides structural salience by construction through required key enumeration, making it an empirical question whether this translates to downstream rare-role F1 gains.

**Step 0 — Motivating Pilot Study (Day 4, 4 GPU-hours)**:
Sample 600 event instances from Qwen3-32B without constraints (standard structured prompting with RAMS/WikiEvents schema descriptions). The expanded sample (~4–5 instances per event type for RAMS's 139 types) enables reliable per-role violation statistics. Measure: entity-type mismatch rate, cardinality violation rate, role hallucination rate, and argument role coverage (proportion of schema roles appearing ≥1 time). Report all four metrics unconditionally. The primary paper argument holds regardless of outcome: low violation rates motivate the structural salience framing (SCG's required key enumeration matters beyond error correction); high rates additionally motivate constraint enforcement for quality improvement. Both are reported; neither determines the primary framing.

**Step 1 — Schema Constraint Grammar (Days 1-3, human engineering)**:
Derive typed constraint specifications from RAMS (cardinality directly from public ontology TSV, encoding the 'count permitted' values as maximum bounds; entity-type compatibility from dataset annotations) and WikiEvents (entity-type compatibility from annotations). Encode as XGrammar-compatible context-free grammars. Critically, all applicable role slots for a given event type are encoded as required keys in the output JSON template: the LLM must generate each role name as a JSON key, and may output an empty string or null value for absent optional arguments, but cannot omit any role key from the output. This required-key design is the structural salience mechanism — it forces the model's attention to each role slot during the forward pass rather than allowing silent omission of rare slots, as occurs in unconstrained generation (Condition A) and is not recoverable by post-hoc filtering (Condition B). Cardinality constraints additionally enforce upper bounds on role-filler counts and entity-type compatibility per filler. RAMS TSV availability substantially reduces construction effort. Scoped to 2 ontologies.

**Step 2 — Three-Condition Data Generation with Volume Control (Days 5-7, ~62.5 GPU-hours)**:
All conditions use Qwen3-32B on 2×A100 80GB via vLLM. **Target training volume**: N = 5,000 event argument instances per condition, distributed proportionally across the 139 RAMS event types (~36 instances per type on average, with a minimum of 1 per rare type) and WikiEvents event types. To eliminate the volume confound — where Condition B (post-hoc filtered) would otherwise train on fewer instances than C — the following volume normalization protocol is applied:

- **Pool Generation**: Generate 1.5× the target volume (7,500 unconstrained instances) as unconstrained instances (same chat prompting with schema descriptions). Report achieved token throughput and generation settings.
- **Condition A (Unconstrained)**: Randomly subsample N=5,000 instances from the 7,500-instance pool.
- **Condition B (Post-hoc Filtered — Oracle Soft Baseline)**: Apply the automated verifier to the full 7,500-instance pool; retain instances passing all entity-type, cardinality, and role-hallucination checks, targeting N=5,000 post-filter instances. Report the achieved discard rate (e.g., 'we generated 7,500 instances and discarded X%, retaining 5,000 for training') as a transparency metric. If the filter discards more than 33% (leaving fewer than 5,000 clean instances), increase the pool to 2× (10,000 instances) and regenerate the additional batch. This baseline approximates oracle-quality soft constraint enforcement without reimplementing LtGaE's RL loop; crucially, it CANNOT recover structural salience for roles absent from filtered instances because unconstrained generation never emitted those role keys.
- **Condition C (SCG-Constrained)**: Grammar-constrained vLLM decoding via XGrammar to exactly N=5,000 instances, enforcing all role-entity-type assignments and cardinality constraints during the forward pass (<40μs/token overhead, per XGrammar MLSys 2025). The grammar's required role-key enumeration in the output template provides structural salience by construction.

All three conditions train on exactly N=5,000 instances, making the C-vs-B comparison methodologically airtight.

**Step 3 — Constraint Verification (concurrent with Step 2)**:
The automated verifier checks all generated instances and reports: filter rate for the A/B pool (transparency metric), corpus-level role coverage for each condition, near-zero filter rate for Condition C (SCG compliance guarantee). Role coverage differences across conditions directly measure the structural salience effect prior to fine-tuning.

**Step 4 — Fine-tuning and Evaluation (Days 8-11, ~57 GPU-hours)**:
LoRA fine-tune Qwen3-8B on each of the three volume-matched corpora (3 conditions × ~15 GPU-hours = 45 GPU-hours). Evaluate zero-shot on WikiEvents and RAMS using LtGaE three-way protocol (RAMS2RAMS, RAMS2Wiki, Wiki2Wiki). Comparison table: LtGaE, ASEE, supervised SOTA (DEGAP), Condition A, Condition B, Condition C. BiTer reported separately under native within-dataset protocol with explicit non-comparability footnote.

**Step 5 — Stratified Evaluation (Day 12, ~12 GPU-hours for inference)**:
The primary analysis section — demonstrates mechanistic explanation of C vs. A/B gaps:
(a) Role Rarity Strata: Rank argument roles by frequency in source schema annotations; partition into quartiles. Report C vs. A and C vs. B F1 for each quartile. Hypothesis: C-B gap concentrates in the bottom quartile (rarest roles) because grammar-guided required key enumeration most strongly prompts the model to instantiate rarely-occurring role types; for common roles, both unconstrained and post-hoc filtered corpora already have sufficient coverage.
(b) Cardinality Tightness Strata: Partition by RAMS-ontology cardinality — max=1 (singleton roles) vs. max>1. Report C vs. A and C vs. B F1 for each partition. Hypothesis: C outperforms B on max=1 roles because Condition B can only remove duplicates but may still have duplicate instances within the filtered corpus; SCG hard-enforces the singleton constraint.
If overall C-B delta is modest (e.g., <1 F1), the stratified analysis provides a theoretically grounded finding even for the Findings track: structural salience helps specifically where theory predicts, at a granularity that soft filtering cannot replicate. Both role coverage rates and argument span F1 are reported per stratum, allowing quality and coverage effects to be distinguished (addressing the concern that grammar-constrained decoding may improve role coverage while degrading span quality).

**Null Result Pre-Specification**:
We pre-specify the null result interpretation in the paper: if C does not outperform B even in the rare-role quartile or singleton-cardinality partition, we report this as a clearly framed negative finding — grammar-guided structural enumeration via required key templates during generation provides no additional rare-role instantiation benefit over oracle post-hoc filtering of unconstrained generation at Qwen3-32B scale. This is a practically useful negative result: it suggests that strong instruction-following models already provide sufficient structural salience through prompt-specified schema descriptions, and that engineering investment in SCG construction may not be warranted at this model scale. EMNLP Findings publishes clearly framed negative results; this pre-specification distinguishes a null result from a failed experiment.

**Limitations and Quality Tradeoffs**:
Grammar-constrained decoding may introduce quality degradation beyond structural coverage: Schall & de Melo (RANLP 2025) demonstrate that constrained decoding forces instruction-tuned models away from high-confidence natural language paths, potentially increasing extraction misses. We mitigate this by using Qwen3-32B (whose strong instruction-following capability reduces divergence between constrained and unconstrained generation paths) and by measuring argument span F1 per role stratum in the stratified evaluation alongside role coverage rates, so that quality and coverage effects are distinguishable rather than conflated.

**Paper writing**: Concurrent from Day 1 (intro, related work, method drafted during experiment runs); intensive final writing Days 13-16.",
